questions.stem: For the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) (forward reaction is exothermic), what happens if the temperature is increased?

options.text: Equilibrium shifts right, producing more ammonia
Equilibrium shifts left, producing less ammonia, to absorb the extra heat
No change because temperature does not affect equilibrium
Equilibrium shifts right because higher temperature always favours products

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle states the system opposes the change. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction (which absorbs heat). Since the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse (endothermic) direction is favoured. The equilibrium shifts left, reducing the yield of ammonia. This is why the Haber process uses a compromise temperature.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), what is the effect of increasing pressure?

options.text: Equilibrium shifts left because there are more moles of gas on the left
Equilibrium shifts right because there are fewer moles of gas on the right
No change because pressure does not affect equilibrium
Equilibrium shifts left to increase the volume

questions.explanation: Left side: 2 + 1 = 3 moles of gas. Right side: 2 moles of gas. Le Chatelier's principle says increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas (to reduce pressure). The equilibrium shifts right towards SO3, increasing yield. This is why high pressure is used in the Contact process.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), what is the effect of increasing pressure?

options.text: Equilibrium shifts right
Equilibrium shifts left
No effect on the equilibrium position because there are equal moles of gas on both sides
The reaction stops completely

questions.explanation: Left side: 1 + 1 = 2 moles of gas. Right side: 2 moles of gas. Since there are equal numbers of moles of gas on both sides, changing pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium. The system cannot reduce pressure by shifting in either direction because both sides have the same number of gas moles.

questions.stem: In the equilibrium: CoCl4²-(aq) + 6H2O(l) ⇌ Co(H2O)6²+(aq) + 4Cl-(aq) (forward reaction is endothermic), the solution is blue when CoCl4²- dominates and pink when Co(H2O)6²+ dominates. Adding more water makes the solution turn pink. Which principle explains this?

options.text: Adding water dilutes the pink colour, making it more visible
Adding water increases the concentration of a reactant, shifting equilibrium to the right
Adding water decreases the temperature, favouring the exothermic direction
Water acts as a catalyst for the forward reaction

questions.explanation: Adding more water increases the concentration of water (a reactant on the left side). Le Chatelier's principle states the system will shift to oppose this increase by using up the extra water. The equilibrium shifts right (forward), producing more Co(H2O)6²+ (pink). This demonstrates how changing concentration affects equilibrium.

questions.stem: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) (exothermic forward), a student says 'we should use the lowest possible temperature to get the most ammonia.' Why is this not practical in industry?

options.text: Low temperature makes the catalyst stop working
Low temperature gives a high equilibrium yield but an unacceptably slow rate of reaction
Low temperature actually favours the reverse reaction
Low temperature causes the gases to liquefy

questions.explanation: While low temperature does shift the equilibrium to the right (favouring NH3), it also drastically reduces the rate of reaction. Very few particles would have enough energy to overcome the activation energy. A compromise temperature of about 450°C is used - high enough for a reasonable rate but not so high that it shifts equilibrium too far left.
